title: VIEWPOINT: The Patient We Didn’t Know How to See
html:
Written by Loren King, RDH

“I thought I was voluntarily doing favors for someone I loved.” “I thought we were making money so we could buy a house and have the family we talked about.” “I didn’t even know what happened to me had a name.” Different humans. Different stories. The same terrifying misunderstanding. They did not believe they were victims of human trafficking.

Before we go any further, I want you to meet two humans. Human #1 was seven years old the first time she was sexually assaulted by an extended family member. Before he assaulted her, he told her, “Say yes to whatever I’m about to ask you to do.” She was seven. So she said yes.

At 21, it happened again with a different extended family member. She needed someone to cosign a student loan. He agreed, then asked for a sexual favor in return. This time she was old enough to talk her way out. Human #1 was not trafficked. Sexual assault and human trafficking are not interchangeable. For some children, however, the story does not stop there. Remember her; we will come back to her.

Human #2 was 12 years old. Her story was told to me early in my career, and I have carried it ever since. I was told she was raped by 56 men over 12 hours and that her trafficker made approximately $60,000 from exploiting one child. Eventually, I was told, she was returned to her parents because her trafficker no longer considered her profitable.

Two weeks later, I was told Human #2 died by suicide. I cannot independently confirm every detail of a story shared with me all those years ago, nor would I compromise the privacy of the human at its center trying to do so. But I can tell you what hearing it did to me. It changed the direction of my life.

I started learning, talking and teaching, then standing in rooms full of healthcare professionals asking them to look closer. This became my life’s purpose. I cannot end human trafficking alone, but I believe one human can change what happens next for another. The story I heard early in my career has stayed with me through every class I teach. It reminds me that the patient whose circumstances we do not understand may be the person who most needs us to pay attention.

You cannot recognize something you have never been taught to see. Awareness is where we start, but awareness without action does not create change. I will hold the light. I need you to walk into the room with me.

What This Has to Do With Dentistry

We sit inches away from another human being. We examine their face, neck, lips, tongue, palate and teeth. We look behind their ears and underneath their jaw. We ask about pain and how injuries happened. We notice when something changes. We are specialists of the head and neck, and violence can leave evidence there.

In one U.S. study of 173 trafficking survivors, 68% reported seeing a healthcare provider while being trafficked. More than one in four, 26.5%, reported seeing a dentist. Patients may sit in our chair, open their mouth and answer our questions without ever saying “trafficked.” That gives us an opportunity, not a mandate to investigate.

Every Person in the Dental Office Has a Role

Your job is to notice, assess, create an opportunity for safety and know what to do next. The front office may notice who controls identification, insurance or the conversation. The dental assistant may notice bruising, injuries or how a patient changes when a companion enters or leaves. The hygienist often has something incredibly valuable: time, familiarity and a detailed view of the head, neck and mouth. The dentist can evaluate findings, support the team and help determine what happens next.

Every role sees a different piece. Together, we collect those pieces, communicate and assess without assuming.

Learning What to See

When I am concerned about a patient, I consider what is happening around them, how they are behaving and what I can physically see. Who came with them, who answers and who holds their ID? Can they answer a simple question without checking someone else’s face first? These are observations, not a diagnosis of trafficking.

Fear does not always look like crying or asking for help. It may appear as compliance, silence, constant apologies or anxiety that seems disproportionate to the situation. A changing story, depression, hopelessness or dissociation may also raise concern. None is exclusive to trafficking; we are collecting information.

Examine the lips, frena, cheeks, palate, tongue, face, ears, jaw and neck for injuries in different stages of healing, burns or patterned injuries suggesting a loop, line, circle, hand, object or bite. Shape, location and the patient’s explanation matter, but a concerning injury is not proof of how it happened.

One finding I spend a lot of time teaching is palatal bruising. You may see pinpoint petechiae, larger ecchymosis or a clustered, diffuse, geometric or circular pattern. Before drawing conclusions, consider its pattern, location and context.

Oral trauma can cause palatal injury. So can violent vomiting, severe coughing, infection, suction or localized trauma. Unusual oral bleeding alongside spontaneous gingival bleeding, unexplained bruising, fatigue or recurrent infections could indicate a hematologic disease, platelet disorder or leukemia.

Imagine two patients with palatal bruising, one following violent vomiting and the other forced oral trauma. Could either of us distinguish the cause from a photograph alone? No. Even if sexual contact caused the finding, tissue cannot tell us whether that contact was consensual. That requires listening to the patient.

In children, pay close attention to bruising. “Those who don’t cruise rarely bruise.” TEN-4-FACESp is a validated clinical decision rule that identifies bruising in young children that warrants further evaluation. TEN directs attention to the torso, ears and neck. FACES includes the frenulum, angle of the jaw, cheeks, eyelids and subconjunctivae. The “p” is patterned bruising.

We examine these areas every day. The tool does not diagnose abuse; it identifies findings that warrant further evaluation. I do not need you to know exactly what happened. I need you to recognize when a second question is warranted.

Responding Without Investigating

If pieces begin lining up, slow down. Get the patient alone if you can do so safely. Do not confront the person you are worried about. Do not interrogate the patient, promise rescue or make decisions for a competent adult because you think you know what is best. Your job is to create the safest opportunity possible for another human to tell you what they want you to know.

That is why I teach PEARR: Provide Privacy, Educate, Ask, Respect and Respond. There is no R for Rescue. A patient may decline help today. Respect that. Six months from now, they may remember the person who said, “If you ever need help, there are people who will believe you.” You may never know what that moment meant. Do it anyway.

And please document objectively. Describe the injury, location, size and appearance. Record exact patient words and conflicting explanations. Take appropriate clinical photographs when permitted and consented to. Do not chart “patient is being trafficked” when you do not know that. Your chart may outlive your memory.

Understanding Human Trafficking

Human trafficking does not require kidnapping, crossing a border or being locked in a room. The trafficker does not have to be a stranger. Under U.S. federal law, trafficking generally involves compelling someone into labor or services, or commercial sex through force, fraud or coercion. Coercion may involve threats, debt, immigration status, housing, money, drugs, fear or someone the person loves.

If someone under 18 is induced to engage in a commercial sex act, federal law does not require proof of force, fraud or coercion. Human trafficking also includes forced labor in agriculture, domestic work, manufacturing, construction, hospitality, restaurants and supply chains. There is no single face of trafficking.

Following the Money

The International Labour Organization estimates forced labor in the private economy generates approximately $236 billion in illegal profits every year. Forced commercial sexual exploitation accounts for about 27% of people in privately imposed forced labor, yet approximately 73% of its illegal profits. In 2022, among trafficking victims detected globally, forced labor represented 42% and sexual exploitation 36%.

Why would somebody stop? Criminology has repeatedly found that the perceived certainty of being caught can deter crime more effectively than simply increasing punishment severity. If profit is enormous, detection is difficult and an exploiter believes nobody will catch them, what have we done to make exploitation a bad business decision? I want trafficking to become a high-risk, low-profit business that is difficult to hide or sustain. We cannot place the entire burden of stopping it on the person being trafficked. That requires attention beyond the clinical encounter. The people who profit from exploitation must face accountability, and the people whose vulnerability they exploit must have access to protection and support.

Our Role as Consumers

Commercial sexual exploitation has buyers, forced labor produces goods and services, and you and I are consumers. The U.S. Department of Labor identifies more than 200 goods from dozens of countries and areas that it has reason to believe are produced with child labor or forced labor. The suffering can disappear long before the product reaches us.

Sexual exploitation has demand, too: someone pays for access to another human being. We spend enormous energy asking why a person didn’t leave. I want us to spend more time asking why another human believed they were entitled to buy them. This does not make an ordinary consumer equally responsible for trafficking. It means trafficking exists inside an ecosystem of profit, demand and vulnerability.

Businesses, buyers, consumers, healthcare professionals, law enforcement, legislators and communities all have a role. Awareness tells us action is necessary.

Examining the Systems

Housing instability, poverty, prior abuse, family rejection, immigration vulnerability, war, displacement, disability and isolation can all create vulnerability. Poverty and childhood trauma do not traffic people; people exploit the vulnerabilities of others. That distinction matters.

Nearly 315,000 minors were legally entered into marriage in the United States between 2000 and 2021. Some were as young as ten. Eighty-six percent were girls, and most were married to adult men. As of this writing in 2026, marriage under 18 remains legal in 32 states. Child marriage is not automatically human trafficking, but we cannot discuss exploitation honestly without examining systems that can leave children vulnerable to coercion, sexual violence, financial dependence and isolation. We are often better at looking for monsters than examining systems.

Taking Awareness Beyond the Operatory

Does your team know what to do if a patient raises concern tomorrow? Create a protocol for safely establishing privacy, learn reporting requirements where you practice, and understand what changes when a patient is a minor or someone is in immediate danger. Train the entire team.

Know the National Human Trafficking Hotline: 1-888-373-7888. Text 233733. Remember that even handing someone a resource requires thought if another person monitors their phone or belongings.

Beyond the operatory, pay attention to legislation, protections for children and training for healthcare professionals. Ask how exploiters are identified and whether companies know what is happening in their supply chains.

Part of my work through Finding Anon is pushing toward a future where healthcare professionals across all 50 states know how to recognize exploitation and respond without creating more harm. I don’t want someone’s chance of being seen to depend on whether their dental professional happened to attend the right conference. Recognition must lead to prevention, survivor services, accountability, education and laws that protect vulnerable people before exploitation happens.

Remember Human Number One

Human #1, the seven-year-old and the 21-year-old, is me. Would you have known by looking at me? Probably not. My story did not become a trafficking story. I was sexually assaulted, not trafficked, and I was fortunate that my story stopped where it did. Another child’s does not.

I waited until now to tell you because I wanted you to spend this article with Human #1 without knowing. That is what happens every day: we clean teeth, take radiographs, joke with patients, ask about their children and schedule their next visit. Underneath everything we can see is an entire life we cannot. Assess. Never assume.

Now You Have the Light

At the beginning, I offered to hold the light if you walked into the room with me. You are here now. I am asking you to see people, to notice, ask, listen, document, respect and respond.

One question, one accurate chart note or one moment of privacy matters. So does one person saying, “I believe you.” One human can change what happens next for another, and then another. Awareness was only ever supposed to be where we started.

At the beginning, I promised I would hold the light. Now you have a light, too. Don’t turn it off.

I love you, mean it.

Ms. King is a global speaker, educator, and founder of Finding Anon. She teaches human trafficking awareness and trauma informed responses in healthcare. She can be reached on Instagram @fromlorenwithlove.

Disclosure: Ms. King reports no disclosures.
